title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-285-479-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-285-479-003
Issues
Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that she
⮚
is entitled to Temporary Total Disability (TTD) benefits from November 15, 20241 until
November 3, 2025.
If Claimant established entitlement to TTD benefits, whether Respondents
⮚
established by a preponderance of the evidence that Claimant was responsible for her
termination of employment on November 13, 2024, and, therefore, pursuant to section
8-43-103(1)(g), C.R.S., is not entitled to TTD.
Stipulation
1. The parties stipulated that Claimant’s average weekly wage is $1070.19.
Findings of Fact
1. Employer sells roof gutter systems meant to protect gutters from becoming
blocked by leaves and other debris.
1 At hearing Claimant’s counsel originally requested the TTD period began on
November 15, 2024. When Respondents stated that Claimant was terminated on
November 13, 2024, Claimant requested to modify her TTD request to November 13,
2024. The evidence admitted at hearing shows that while Claimant was terminated on
November 13, 2024, she was paid through November 14, 2024. Ex. I. Therefore, the
ALJ concludes that if Claimant is entitled to TTD benefits, the TTD period should begin
November 15, 2024, the first day she was no longer paid by Employer.
1

2. Claimant was hired by Employer on September 21, 2022. Claimant was originally
hired as a promoter working home shows; Claimant was later promoted to field event
marketing manager. Claimant’s job duties included scheduling field events, working field
events, and hiring promoters for field events. While working at field events, Claimant
was required to set up and take down displays including items weighing up to 30
pounds.
3. Claimant suffered an admitted work injury to her lower back on March 27, 2024.
Claimant was ultimately given work restrictions of lifting no more than 10 pounds.
4. Claimant was given job performance goals based in part on the number of leads
she produced at field events. Particularly, Claimant was to meet certain goals
concerning the cost per lead, which cost included the cost of the field event generating
the leads.
5. Claimant’s work restrictions increased Claimant’s cost per lead, as she had to
hire a promoter to help set up and take down displays at field events and the cost of that
promoter was factored into the cost per lead. Prior to her work injury, Claimant was able
to work field events on her own, lowering the cost per lead.
6. Claimant was unable to meet her cost-per-lead job performance goals both
before and after her work injury. Claimant received two disciplinary actions for not
meeting her performance goals.
7. Claimant was terminated by Employer on November 13, 2024.
8. Claimant credibly testified that at the time she was terminated she was told
Employer had eliminated all field event marketing manager positions across the country.
9. Clayton Stackpole, Employer’s Director of Event Marketing during the time period
in question, testified for Respondents. Mr. Stackpole indirectly supervised Claimant and
was in weekly contact with Claimant’s direct supervisor Joey Egbert. Mr. Stackpole
testified that Claimant received written warnings in October 2023 and May 2024 for not
meeting her performance goals.
2

10. Mr. Stackpole testified that field event marketing managers were expected to
generate leads at a cost of less than $400.00 per lead. Claimant was generating leads
at a cost of more than $600.00 per lead. This was the reason for Claimant’s written
warnings. In his opinion, Claimant was terminated for failure to meet her performance
metrics, not because the position of field event marketing manager was eliminated by
Employer.
11. Mr. Stackpole testified that some of the job duties previously performed by field
event marketing managers are now completed remotely by regional managers for
Employer.
12. Employer’s records show the “main reason for the separation of this employee” is
“Position Elimination.” Ex. I.
13. Under “provide more information on the separation reason” Mr. Stackpole wrote
“[p]erformance and documentation throughout the year as well as position elimination in
this branch for restructure plans into 2025 due to performance[.]” Ex. I.
14. Under “Transaction Change History” the “select main reason for the separation of
this employee” was changed from “Unsatisfactory performance” to “Position
Elimination.” Ex. I. That change was made by and was approved by
. Id.
15. In an email to , Mr. Stackpole wrote that he spoke to Claimant telling
her that “due to performance the department in this location has been struggling to be
profitable as a business” and “Colorado along with some others are removing the local
FEM role from the location and will be operated by a senior level manager as it was in
the past prior to the introduction of the FEM role and a reduction in event operations
and activity.” Ex. I (emphasis added). Attached to the email from Mr. Stackpole is an
email from Mr. Egbert sent at 12:22 AM of the day of Claimant’s termination stating
“Here is what I dug up for . I feel like there is more, but this is what i could easily
locate.” Id.
3

16. Based on the documentary evidence provided by Respondents, the ALJ finds it
more likely than not that Employer was eliminating Claimant’s position and sought a
pretextual performance reason for her termination by “digging up” Claimant’s previous
disciplinary actions before telling her she was being let go on November 13, 2024.
17. Claimant was placed at maximum medical improvement on November 3, 2025.
18. Claimant credibly testified that she did not work between November 13, 2024 and
November 3, 2025.
19. The ALJ gives little weight to Mr. Stackpole’s testimony that the reason Claimant
was terminated was because of her performance rather than elimination of the position
by Employer.
20. The ALJ finds the documentary evidence listing Claimant’s reason for separation
as “Position Elimination” persuasive.
21. A preponderance of the evidence supports a finding that Claimant was
terminated from her position because the position was eliminated by Employer.
22. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled
to temporary total disability benefits from November 15, 2024 to November 3, 2025.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Act is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability
and medical benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S.
B. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving entitlement to benefits by a
preponderance of the evidence. § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is
that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact
is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197 Colo. 306, 318 (1979).
4

C. The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted neutrally –
neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of the respondents
– and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
D. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
Univ. Park Care Ctr. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637, 641 (Colo. App. 2001).
Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it is for
the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and draw
plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. When determining credibility, the fact finder
should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's
testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or
improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the
testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Bodensieck v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 183 P.3d 684, 687 (Colo. App. 2008).
E. The ALJ’s factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of evidence or
every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected evidence
contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App. 2000).
TTD
F. “Temporary disability benefits are intended to compensate a claimant for actual
wages lost during the time the claimant is unable to work because of injury.” PDM
Molding v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542, 548 (Colo. 1995). To prove entitlement to TTD
benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more
than three work shifts, that he or she left work as a result of the disability, and that the
disability resulted in an actual wage loss. § 8-42-103(1), C.R.S.; § 8-42-105(1), C.R.S.;
see City of Colo. Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d 637, 639 (Colo. App.
1997).
5

G. Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S., requires the claimant to establish a causal
connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain
TTD benefits. Lindner Chevrolet v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 914 P.2d 496, 498 (Colo.
App. 1995). The term “disability” connotes two elements: (1) medical incapacity
evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning
capacity as demonstrated by claimant’s inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver
v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity
element of disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant’s ability effectively and properly to perform his or her regular
employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo. App. 1998).
Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce evidence of medical
restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability.
Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997).
H. TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the following: (1)
the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or modified
employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written release to return
to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the employee a written
release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered in writing, and the
employee fails to begin the employment. § 8-42-105(3)(a)-(d), C.R.S.
I. Employers or insurers must pay statutory interest of 8% per annum on all
benefits not paid when due. § 8-43-410(2), C.R.S.; see Subsequent Inj. Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 859 P.2d 276, 278 (Colo. App. 1993).
J. Here, Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence that she had a
disability lasting more than three work shifts, Claimant was separated from her
employment by elimination of her position by Employer, and Claimant was out of work
from the time she was terminated until she reached MMI on November 3, 2025.
Accordingly, the ALJ concludes that Claimant has established her entitlement to TTD
benefits from November 15, 2024 to November 3, 2025.
6

Responsible for Termination
K. “In cases where it is determined that a temporarily disabled employee is
responsible for termination of employment, the resulting wage loss shall not be
attributable to the on-the-job injury.” § 8-42-103(1)(g), C.R.S.; § 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S.
Accordingly, a claimant who is responsible for the termination of employment is not
entitled to temporary disability benefits absent a worsening of condition which
reestablishes the causal connection between the injury and the wage loss. Anderson v.
Longmont Toyota, Inc., 102 P.3d 323, 330 (Colo. 2004); see Grisbaum v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 109 P.3d 1054, 1056 (Colo. App. 2005).
L. The dispositive question in these cases is whether the employee performed a
volitional act or otherwise exercised a degree of control over the circumstances
resulting in her discharge. Poos v. Murfin Drilling Co., W.C. No. 5-185-172-002 (ICAO,
Jan. 17, 2025) (citing Colo. Springs Disposal v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 58 P.3d 1061
(Colo. App. 2002); Padilla v. Digital Equip. Corp., 902 P.2d 414 (Colo. App. 1994)
opinion after remand 908 P.2d 1185 (Colo. App. 1995); Colo. Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 18 P.3d 790 (Colo. App. 2000)).
M. Because sections 8-42-103(1)(g), C.R.S., and 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S., provide a
defense to an otherwise valid claim for temporary disability benefits, respondents
shoulder the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the claimant
was responsible for her termination and subsequent wage loss. Poos v. Murfin Drilling
Co., W.C. No. 5-185-172-002 (ICAO, Jan. 17, 2025).
N. A preponderance of the evidence supports the conclusion that Claimant was not
responsible for her termination because Employer eliminated Claimant’s position at the
time Employer terminated Claimant. Indeed, Employer’s own paperwork states that
Claimant was terminated because her position was eliminated. Because the elimination
of Claimant’s position was not a volitional act resulting in her discharge, Respondents
have failed to establish Claimant was responsible for her termination. Accordingly,
Respondents are responsible for paying Claimant TTD benefits from November 15,
2024 to November 3, 2025.
7

Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant is entitled to temporary total disability benefits from November 15, 2024
to November 3, 2025.
All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
